author: DoctoRx
title: Introduction When Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A ) ( BRK.B
text:
Introduction When Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRK.A ) ( BRK.B ) made Apple ( AAPL ) a major, core holding not long ago, it added another multinational stock to its portfolio. But operationally, in its insurance operations and major corporate subsidiaries, Berkshire is very much a US-centric company.
AAPL may now be joining its most famous and influential shareholder in again becoming more US-centric. The catalyst: the tax bill. The US has joined most of the rest of the world with a humble tax policy. When AAPL earns money in the EU, or Brazil, it now pays no tax penalty for its foreign subsidiary to pay a dividend to the parent. This money can now go to shareholders, or it can be invested in the US.
The other part of the deal, as you very likely know, is that the federal tax rate for business transacted in the US is now 21%, down sharply from 35%. In addition, the GILTI provision in the tax act, which sets a "Minimum tax on 'global intangible low-taxed income'' per KPMG , may diminish the attractiveness of setting up new facilities in Ireland or other tax havens.
I expect that AAPL is going to be, again, a trendsetter in increasing its operations in the US.
So, as the framers of the tax bill hoped, corporations domiciled in the US (and elsewhere) have greater incentives now to expand in the US. They are finally not penalized by high corporate tax rates, GILTI may affect placing intellectual property in Ireland, and profits generated ex-US can come back to the mother ship without US penalty.
Thus, the future pattern of investment in the US by corporations is going to be revealed this year and next. I believe that seeing is believing, and that investors are marking US stocks up with a rational basis
